title: Dominic and the Bakery
premise: For ten years, Tamsin Okonkwo has survived her father's death, a failing vineyard, and mounting debts on the strength of unsigned letters that arrived every month — letters she believes were written by her late mother. When Dominic Reyes opens a bakery next door, he carries a secret: he was the boy her mother hired, then kept writing after she died because stopping felt like a second abandonment. As Tamsin's lease and his collide with a developer's offer that could save them both at the cost of each other, Dominic must finally speak the confession he has rehearsed for a decade. In the end, truth costs Tamsin the comfort of the letters but gives her something sturdier: a partner who chooses her with full knowledge of what he owes, and a vineyard reborn as a bakery-and-wine cooperative.
about_author: Cyrus Zhou is the pen name of a former pastry chef who traded pre-dawn ovens for pre-dawn manuscripts and writes love stories set in small businesses on the edge of ruin. They live in wine country with a sourdough starter older than most of their relationships.

chapters.title: The Last Letter
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. On the tenth anniversary of the letters, Tamsin rereads every one while creditors circle her inherited vineyard. She notices the handwriting shifted subtly years ago but refuses to ask why. Emotional beat: tender denial — the letters are the only inheritance she trusts.

chapters.title: Flour Next Door
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. Dominic signs the lease on the shuttered bakery adjoining Okonkwo Vineyards, telling himself proximity is coincidence. His first sight of Tamsin — arguing with a bank notice in the rain — undoes ten years of rehearsed composure. Beat: dread braided with longing.

chapters.title: Bread for the Harvest
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Desperate for harvest-festival revenue, Tamsin swallows pride and asks the new baker to supply her tasting event. Dominic agrees too quickly, and she mistakes his eagerness for pity. Beat: prickly alliance formed out of mutual need.

chapters.title: What Mother Paid For
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. A flashback chapter: sixteen-year-old Dominic, hired by Grace Okonkwo to draft letters when her illness stole her strength, then continuing alone after her death because Tamsin's replies were the warmest thing in his life. Beat: guilt revealed to the reader, not the heroine.

chapters.title: The Developer's Card
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Marcus Hale, a developer, offers to erase Tamsin's debts if she sells — and mentions, casually, that he already owns the bakery building's lease. Tamsin realizes her neighbor's future is as fragile as hers. Beat: the ground shifts under both of them.

chapters.title: Sourdough Confessions
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. Late-night baking session; Tamsin appears unable to sleep, and they trade half-truths over proofing dough. She tells him about the letters; he nearly confesses and instead teaches her to score a loaf. Beat: intimacy deepening around the secret like steam around a lid.

chapters.title: A Reply Ten Years Late
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Inspired by feeling seen for the first time, Tamsin writes a reply to the letters and leaves it at the bakery, asking Dominic — as a stranger — whether she's foolish to trust an unknown hand for a decade. Beat: dramatic irony tightening like a tourniquet.

chapters.title: Hale Makes It Official
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. Marcus offers Dominic a deal: endorse the sale to Tamsin, keep his lease. Dominic refuses and loses his renewal option — ninety days until eviction. Beat: duty and love begin pulling in opposite directions.

chapters.title: The Festival Fire
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. The harvest festival succeeds — their joint bread-and-wine table draws crowds — until a small kitchen fire (minor, but public) lets Marcus whisper that the pair together are a liability. Beat: triumph curdling into doubt.

chapters.title: Letters I Never Sent
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. Dominic drafts a confession letter, then burns it in the bread oven. His sister Rosa confronts him: 'You've been brave by mail for ten years. Be brave in person.' Beat: the cost of silence made explicit.

chapters.title: The Archive Box
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Sorting her mother's things for a forced inventory, Tamsin finds a receipt: payments to 'D. Reyes, correspondence.' She doesn't connect it — yet — but pockets it, unsettled. Beat: suspicion planted like a dormant vine.

chapters.title: Ninety Days, Sixty Left
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Working side by side to save both businesses, Tamsin and Dominic cross from partners into something unspoken. A near-kiss is interrupted by a creditor's call. Beat: love arriving at the worst possible time.

chapters.title: Rosa Spills
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Rosa, furious at her brother's cowardice, tells Tamsin that Dominic 'has been writing to someone in this valley for a decade.' Tamsin, holding the receipt, goes cold. Beat: the secret surfaces without its meaning yet complete.

chapters.title: Confrontation at the Ovens
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Tamsin demands the truth. Dominic admits the letters are his — but frames it as mercy, and Tamsin hears theft: even her grief had been managed by someone else. Beat: first-act wound reopened; she walks out.

chapters.title: The Empty Kitchen
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. Dominic stops baking, stops writing, prepares to leave quietly when the lease ends. Rosa forces him to reread Tamsin's childhood replies — and one line: 'Whoever you are, don't ever stop.' Beat: rock bottom, and the shape of redemption visible in it.

chapters.title: Marcus Closes In
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. With the festival momentum gone, Marcus pressures Tamsin to sign, dangling debt forgiveness. Alone, she rereads the letters with new eyes and sees, finally, not deception but devotion — a boy who kept a promise no one asked him to keep. Beat: anger transmuting into understanding.

chapters.title: The Sentence Rehearsed
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. Eviction day. Instead of packing, Dominic walks into the vineyard during the final tasting event and says the sentence he has rehearsed for ten years: 'Your mother didn't write the letters. I did — and I never stopped because loving you was the truest thing I ever did.' Beat: climax; the truth spoken at last.

chapters.title: What Truth Buys
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Stunned, Tamsin doesn't answer — she signs nothing, sells nothing, and instead uses the letters' decade of dates to prove the vineyard's steady value, buying time from the bank. Beat: the heroine reclaiming agency using the very history she thought was stolen.

chapters.title: Lease and Loaf
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Tamsin negotiates with Marcus: she'll sell him a minority stake in a reimagined venture — vineyard tastings supplied by the bakery next door — if he transfers Dominic's lease to her name. Beat: love against duty resolved into partnership.

chapters.title: The First Honest Letter
chapters.summary: Dominic's POV. Dominic writes Tamsin a signed letter — no anonymity left — and delivers it by hand. She reads it standing in his kitchen, flour on her hands, and answers aloud instead of by post. Beat: quiet reconciliation, earned rather than granted.

chapters.title: Harvest, Second Pressing
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. One year later: the cooperative's opening day, the old vines pruned back to bear again. Tamsin pins the first letter — the original, unsigned — above the counter as a reminder of where mercy began. Beat: identity rebuilt from loyalty and truth alike.

chapters.title: Dominic and the Bakery
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Closing scene: dawn, ovens warming, two names on the lease. Tamsin asks what he would have written if she'd never found out; Dominic hands her a fresh letter, sealed, dated ten years from today. Beat: resolution as continuation — love as a promise still being written.
